stem: A 5-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department due to recurrent seizures over the past 24 hours.  The patient has been having high fever and flu-like symptoms for the past 3 days.  Medical history includes febrile seizures at age 2.  He takes no medications and has no family history of epilepsy.  Temperature is 39.4 C (102.9 F), blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg, pulse is 112/min, and respirations are 22/min.  The patient appears lethargic and does not follow simple commands consistently.  His neck is supple.  During the examination, he suddenly develops episodes of sustained, generalized tonic-clonic convulsions without fully regaining consciousness between them.  An intravenous medication is administered urgently and results in rapid termination of the seizures.  Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action responsible for the therapeutic effect of this medication?​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌​​​​​​​​‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌​​​‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​​‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​​​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​​​​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​​‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​​‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌​​​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌​​​​​​​

options.label: A
options.text: Blockade of presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels

options.label: B
options.text: Blockade of presynaptic voltage-gated sodium channels

options.label: E
options.text: Inhibition of vesicle fusion and neurotransmitter release

explanation:
This patient has status epilepticus (eg, prolonged [≥5 min] or sustained episodes [≥2 seizures] with incomplete recovery) likely secondary to complex febrile seizures or infectious meningitis/encephalitis.  Regardless of etiology, medication for seizure termination should be administered to prevent brain damage; the initial drug of choice for treating status epilepticus is an intravenous benzodiazepine (eg, lorazepam) due to its efficacy and very rapid onset of action.

Benzodiazepines enhance the effect of the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA at the GABA A receptor, a ligand-gated ion channel.  Allosteric attachment of benzodiazepines to the GABA A receptor increases the influx of negatively charged chloride ions in response to GABA binding.  This leads to hyperpolarization of the postsynaptic neuron and suppression of action potential firing (antiseizure effect).

(Choice A)  Presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels mediate the influx of calcium into the axon terminal, promoting vesicle fusion and neurotransmitter release into the synaptic cleft.  Gabapentin can be used as an antiseizure medication; it works by inhibiting voltage-gated calcium channels, thereby attenuating excitatory neurotransmitter release.

(Choice B)  Presynaptic voltage-gated sodium channels open when the cell becomes sufficiently depolarized, triggering an action potential that propagates down the axon.  Phenytoin inhibits voltage-gated sodium channels and decreases the risk for recurrent seizure by increasing the seizure threshold; it has a much slower onset of action compared to benzodiazepines.  Therefore, patients in status epilepticus should be first given a rapid-acting benzodiazepine to abort the seizure as well as a long-acting anticonvulsant such as phenytoin to prevent seizure recurrence.

(Choice D)  Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors are examples of medications that prevent presynaptic neurotransmitter reuptake.  They are typically used to treat depression and anxiety disorders.

(Choice E)  Levetiracetam works by binding to SV2A proteins on synaptic vesicles, directly inhibiting vesicle fusion and excitatory neurotransmitter release into the synaptic cleft.  It decreases the risk for seizure but does so more slowly than a benzodiazepine.

Educational objective:Intravenous benzodiazepines (eg, lorazepam) are the initial drug of choice for status epilepticus.  They work by enhancing the effect of GABA at the GABA A receptor, leading to increased chloride influx and suppression of action potential firing.​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌​​​​​​​​‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌​​​‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​​‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​​​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​​​​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​​‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​​‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌​​​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌​​​​​​​
